newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian president backs PM amid political crisis.
newsitem.headline: Latvian president backs PM amid political crisis.

text.p: Latvian President Guntis Ulmanis backed his prime minister on Tuesday amid a political crisis that threatens to topple the government.
Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Andris Shkele presented a plan to squabbling parties aimed at quelling the crisis, sparked by a spate of cabinet resignations over anti-corruption laws.
Shkele, a tough former businessman, is credited with almost single-handedly speeding up the reforms Latvia launched after quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991.
"I consider that this government led by this prime minister should continue the work it started until the next parliamentary election (in October 1998)," Ulmanis told a news conference.
Ulmanis said the current turmoil threatened the reform process and bids to join both NATO and the European Union (EU).
Shkele's unwieldy seven-party coalition, a rainbow group of nationalists and moderate right and left-wingers, has been threatened by a wave of resignations in recent months.
Shkele said he presented a plan to the cabinet to maintain the coalition's survival.
"I have presented a concrete programme (to the ruling parties) on how to overcome the current problems," Shkele said.

Three ministers quit amid allegations of corruption. A fourth, Interior Minister Dainis Turlais, resigned after eight children plunged to their deaths at a firefighting show when the basket they were in fell from a crane.

Shkele on Monday demanded the resignation of a fifth cabinet member, Transport Minister Vilis Krishtopans, on the grounds that he had violated anti-corruption legislation by holding state and private jobs simultaneously.
Shkele called on the parties to nominate new candidates to fill the vacant posts and proposed an extraordinary session of parliament on August 6 to vote for the new ministers.
He said that the full details of his plan would be made public on Wednesday.
The frequent bouts of political infighting have not prevented Shkele from speeding up market reforms in the small former Soviet republic.
He pushed a balanced budget through the fractious 100-seat parliament, forged ahead with the sale of key state assets and helped pull down inflation.
